author: William Saville

title: A Door Without a Lock
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
Danse had installed three new locks by breakfast.

I discovered this when I tried to bring a crate of replacement fittings into the Brasswatch workshop and couldn't open the side door.

I knocked.

Nothing.

I knocked harder.

Danse appeared on the other side, carrying a wrench.

"You're early," he said.

"The door is locked."

"Yes."

"With three locks."

"Two locks and a secondary latch."

"That is a very helpful distinction."

He took the crate before I dropped it, then stepped aside to let me in.

The workshop smelled of oil, clean metal, and the faint dry heat of the furnace. On the back bench lay the repaired purifier parts, still waiting for final clearance. Ash had left a note asking whether the shelf we'd fixed could hold heavier supplies. Pip had placed a basket of bread beside the window.

Everything looked normal except the door.

"Why?" I asked.

Danse set down the crate.

"Security."

"Against what?"

"Unauthorized entry."

"Who is authorized?"

He looked at me as if the answer were obvious.

"People with permission."

"How do they get permission if the door is locked and you can't hear them?"

He glanced toward the window. For the first time, he seemed to notice that the new latch sat above shoulder height for several people who used the workshop.

"It needs a bell," he said.

"It needs a plan."

We had agreed to make the workshop accessible after Edda's comments at the bridge meeting. Ash had asked for a room that could lock from the inside without requiring anyone to explain their identity. Tamsin wanted to be sure repairs wouldn't block the emergency exit. Danse had focused on keeping everyone safe from the possibility of a hostile visitor.

His solution made half the ordinary visitors feel as though they were approaching a checkpoint.

"I don't want to make this place unsafe," he said.

"Neither do I."

"Then why are you criticizing the locks?"

"Because safety is more than keeping people out."

He rubbed his forehead.

"I know that in theory."

"Then let's test it in practice."

We invited Edda, Tamsin, Pip, and Ash to look at the entrance before any more work began. Danse was uncomfortable with so many people examining something he'd built. He did not complain.

Edda arrived first.

She looked at the raised threshold, the narrow turn inside the door, and the three different mechanisms controlling the lock.

"How do I get through?" she asked.

Danse stepped forward.

"I can assist."

"That's not what I asked."

He stopped.

She measured the opening with a folding ruler.

"The door swings inward. If somebody's already standing by the first bench, there's no clear room. I can't open the top latch from my chair. And if there's a fire, I'm not waiting for the tall man with the keys."

Danse wrote it down.

Ash studied the side window.

"Can anyone see inside the private workroom from here?"

"Yes," Danse said.

"Then it isn't private."

He wrote that down too.

Tamsin tapped the door frame.

"Your reinforcing plate blocks the emergency release."

Danse looked genuinely startled.

"It shouldn't."

"It does."

Pip, who had come to the workshop many times to deliver supplies, asked how someone with their hands full was supposed to announce themselves.

Danse looked at the bell rope he'd begun installing.

"We need to adjust the design."

"Quite a bit," I said.

He gave me a look.

"Yes. Quite a bit."

By lunch, we had a list of requirements instead of a collection of assumptions. The public workshop needed a wide, low-effort entrance, level approach, clear sightlines, and an accessible bell or signaling panel. The private repair room needed a lock controlled by the person inside, plus a way to request help that didn't reveal the reason for the request.

The storage area could remain secured, but only staff needed to use it. The emergency exit could not depend on finding Danse.

We drew the revised layout on the big worktable.

He measured each doorway twice.

I liked watching him work when he'd stopped trying to be perfect. His concentration made a small line between his brows. He didn't talk much. When he disagreed, he pointed to the specific measurement instead of invoking rank.

Ash came over from the private workroom carrying the old latch in a paper bag. She set it on the table so carefully that even Danse noticed.

"Can I have a different one?" she asked.

He looked at the metal. "It's still functional."

"From your side of the door."

He opened his mouth, then shut it. I could see him measuring the distance to the inside handle in his head. He'd spent the morning checking width and clearance; he hadn't asked how the mechanism felt to someone who needed to close it without calling a stronger person over.

Ash showed him. She was shorter than he was, and when she turned the stiff catch her wrist bent awkwardly. She tried again before he could offer to do it for her.

"I can work here," she said. "I just don't want the price of privacy to be a lock I can't use."

Danse's jaw tightened. For a heartbeat I thought he would defend the design because he'd built it. Instead he took a pencil and wrote *operable by occupant* beside the drawing.

"Will you choose the replacement?" he asked.

"I'd like to try the options first."

"Very well."

I watched him cross out the old lock without striking through the whole plan. The thing he'd made wasn't worthless because someone found a flaw in it. It was simply unfinished.

Ash looked at me. "Does he always look like he's been sentenced when someone asks for a change?"

"Only when it involves hardware."

Danse gave me a long, injured look.

"Untrue," he said. "I have accepted several changes to the lighting plan."

"After arguing about all of them."

"Those were technical discussions."

Ash laughed, the sound bright in the workshop. Danse didn't smile, but the furrow between his brows eased.

Later, while Edda prepared the ramp test, he stood beside me and brushed my fingers with his. He rarely made a performance out of tenderness. The small movement had all the weight of him saying he wanted me close without deciding that I needed to be.

"I should have asked her first," he said.

"You did ask her now."

"After she had to ask me."

"Then remember it next time."

He nodded. I didn't give him an absolution he hadn't requested. We had a ramp to test and a new latch to find.

Edda tested the first temporary ramp that afternoon.

It was too steep.

Danse looked dismayed.

"Let's change the angle," she said.

"That will require moving the outer step."

"Then move it."

He knelt beside the stone.

"Right."

The second attempt was better, but the turning space was still too narrow. Tamsin helped shift a bench. Ash built a folding shelf so supplies could be set down without blocking the route.

At dusk, we opened the door for another test.

Edda entered without waiting for anyone to carry her over the threshold.

Danse was silent.

"Now," she said, "we need to make sure it still works when it rains."

He nodded.

"Tomorrow."

I thought he might be disappointed that there was no neat ending.

Instead he seemed relieved to have a real next step.

After the others left, he stood beneath the new bell cord.

"I thought I was protecting people," he said.

"You were trying to."

"That's not the same."

"No."

He looked toward the private room, where Ash had asked us not to install an external viewing panel.

"In the Brotherhood, everything began with securing the perimeter. After that, we decided who was allowed inside."

"And here?"

"Here the people who use the place get to help decide what safe means."

I leaned against the workbench.

"That seems like progress."

He studied me.

"You don't have to reassure me."

"I wasn't. I was observing."

He smiled faintly.

"You're getting good at that."

He took the last tool from the bench and put it away. The movements were slower than usual. I could see fatigue settling in the way he held his shoulders.

"Come home," I said.

"I still need to check the hinges."

"Tomorrow."

He looked tempted to argue.

Then he set the wrench down.

"All right."

Outside, the lanterns along Brasswatch Yard were coming on one by one. The air smelled of damp stone and bread from the square. He took my hand when I offered it.

At the door, he stopped.

"Can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"If I build a place where people can leave without asking permission, will they still come back?"

I turned toward him.

"Some will. Some won't. That's what makes coming back a choice."

He looked toward the open entrance.

"That is not a comfortable answer."

"No. But it's an honest one."

He lifted my hand and kissed it, then leaned close enough for me to feel the warmth of his breath.

"I want you to come back," he said.

"I know."

"Is that too much to ask?"

"No. As long as it's a request."

He smiled, and I kissed him beneath the new bell cord. We went home before the rain arrived.

The following morning, the workshop was open at its usual hour. The old top latch had been removed. The private room had a lock Ash could operate from inside, and the emergency exit opened with one motion.

The place was not finished.

But it was beginning to belong to the people who needed it, not just the man who had built the locks.
